newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Airbus silent on status change delay report.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Airbus silent on status change delay report.

text.p: European aircraft consortium Airbus said late on Sunday it could not confirm or deny a German newspaper report that plans to change the aircraft partnership into an integrated commercial company had been put on hold.

But as the left swept to power in Sunday's French election, Airbus's domestic partner, state-owned Aerospatiale, was likely to see its position reinforced in the French and European aerospace sector, an industry source said.

Germany's Welt am Sonntag reported on Sunday that Airbus Industrie's supervisory board had decided at a May 27 meeting in Toulouse, France, to freeze the strategic change in status that had been announced in January.
"I have no information to confirm or deny this report," an Airbus spokesman said.
The German newspaper, noting the meeting's results had not yet been made public, said talks had become bogged down over how to split up the mix of civil and military programmes.
An industry source said the German report appeared to be an exercise in testing the response of the Airbus partners. "It looks like the Germans are flying a kite," he said.
Relations between the Airbus partners have been strained while the restructuring talks have been going on.
Airbus is a partnership between Aerospatiale, British Aerospace Plc, Daimler-Benz Aerospace, a unit of Daimler-Benz AG, and Construcciones Aeronauticas SA (CASA) of Spain.
It does not publish accounts and passes trading surpluses to its partners to repay government launch aid, and pays them in their capacity as both suppliers and shareholders.

Dasa and BAe, both private companies, have been keen to push ahead with the restructuring, needed to make it more competitive and to face up to a pending merger between archrival Boeing and McDonnell Douglas.

But Aerospatiale has been focusing on a planned merger with combat plane maker Dassault Aviation, which would make it bigger and give it more clout in the Airbus talks. It also takes a more conservative view of the assets to be vested in the new Airbus company.

Aerospatiale's chairman Yves Michot lashed out recently in a French newspaper interview against long-time partner Dasa after the German firm signed agreements with French conglomerate Lagardere to set up missile and space joint ventures.
The Dasa-Lagardere deals amounted to signing the "death warrant" for Airbus, Michot said. Aerospatiale had been in talks for the last three years to form similar ventures with Dasa.

The balance of power among Airbus partners and the outlook for the Dassault/Aerospatiale merger may also be complicated by Sunday's French parliamentary election results, which showed the Socialists and allies ousting the centre-right government, the industry source said.

The Socialists are hostile to privatisations and a planned Aerospatiale sell-off may be cancelled, which would put the state-owned group in a position of strength. "Aerospatiale has the upper hand, it can call the shots," the source said.

Michot wants the European aerospace industry to be restructured to have integrated civil and military wings, along the lines of its U.S. rivals which will have long-term government defence contracts to even out the market cycles for passenger aircraft.
But there was no reason why such a move should rule out a status change for Airbus, which has a stronger element of integration than the fragmented defence sector, the source said.
The Airbus partners signed a memorandum of understanding in January to change its status to a limited liability company, owning its own assets by 1999.
